{{short description|British physicist and academic}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
[[File:Fred Taylor in his Oxford office, March 2016.jpg|thumbnail|Professor Taylor in March 2016]]
'''Fredric William Taylor''' (24 September 1944 – 16 December 2021) was a British [[physicist]] and academic. He was Halley Professor of [[Physics]] Emeritus at the [[University of Oxford]],<ref>{{cite news|title=Fred Taylor: A glimpse of my own future, and a girl to boot|url=http://www.timeshighereducation.co.uk/news/fred-taylor-a-glimpse-of-my-own-future-and-a-girl-to-boot/202273.article|accessdate=31 March 2014|newspaper=Times Higher Education|date=31 March 2006}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=David Bates Medal: Prof Fred Taylor|url=http://www.egu.eu/awards-medals/david-bates/2005/fred-w-taylor/|publisher=European Geophysical Union|accessdate=25 March 2016}}</ref> where he lived until his death.

==Early life and education==
Taylor was born 24 September 1944 in [[Amble]], [[Northumberland]], England.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Read |first1=Peter |last2=Pierrehumbert |first2=Ray |author-link2=Raymond Pierrehumbert |date=2022-06-01 |title=Fred Taylor |url=https://academic.oup.com/astrogeo/article/63/3/3.11/6586418 |journal=[[Astronomy & Geophysics]] |language=en |volume=63 |issue=3 |pages=3.11 |doi=10.1093/astrogeo/atac033 |issn=1366-8781|url-access=subscription }}</ref> His father, William, was a [[joiner]] who had been wounded in [[World War II]], and his mother, Ena, was a teacher. In 1949, the family moved to [[Howick, Northumberland|Howick]], Northumberland.<ref name=Ambler>{{cite web|title=Stargazing fans, meet Amble's own space man|url=http://www.theambler.co.uk/2012/12/14/from-amble-to-mars/|website=The Ambler|accessdate=15 December 2015|date=14 December 2012}}</ref> He was educated at The Duke's School, then an all-boys school in [[Alnwick]].<ref name=Ambler /><ref>{{cite web|title=The History of The Duke's Middle School|url=http://www.dukes.northumberland.sch.uk/website/our_school/133557|website=The Duke's Middle School, Alnwick|accessdate=15 December 2015}}</ref> He studied [[physics]] at the [[University of Liverpool]], graduating with a [[first class honours|first class]] [[Bachelor of Science]] (BSc) degree.<ref name="bio - Amazon">{{cite web|title=F. W. Taylor|url=https://www.amazon.co.uk/F.-W.-Taylor/e/B001IZ1IVG/ref=ntt_dp_epwbk_0|website=Amazon.co.uk|accessdate=16 March 2016}}</ref> He then undertook [[postgraduate research]] in [[atmospheric physics]] at [[Jesus College, Oxford]] under the [[Doctoral supervisor|supervision]] of [[Sir John Houghton]], and graduated from the [[University of Oxford]] with a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] (DPhil) degree.<ref name=Ambler /><ref name="bio - Amazon" />

==Academic career==
In 1970, Taylor joined the [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]] of the [[California Institute of Technology]].<ref name="Ambler" /><ref name="bio - Oxford Physics" /> He was [[principal investigator]] for the first experiment into the [[meteorology]] of the [[atmosphere of Venus]], building an instrument for the [[Pioneer Venus Orbiter]] that launched in 1978.<ref name="bio - Amazon" /> Arriving at Venus in December 1978, this included the first British-built hardware to travel to another planet.<ref name=Venusbook>{{cite book |last1=Taylor |first1=Fredric W. |title=The scientific exploration of Venus |date=2014 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |isbn=978-1107023482}}</ref>  He was also involved in the mission that sent the unmanned spacecraft [[Galileo (spacecraft)|''Galileo'']] to study [[Jupiter]] and [[Moons of Jupiter|its moons]].<ref name="bio - Amazon" />

In 1980, he returned to Oxford University where he became Professor and Head of Department.<ref name=Ambler /> Under his leadership, the Group was involved in space missions to study the atmospheres of Earth, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn and Titan, as well as Mercury, the Moon, and a comet.<ref name=Memoir>{{cite book|last1=Taylor|first1=Fred|title=Exploring the Planets: A Memoir|date=2016|publisher=Oxford University Press|location=Oxford|isbn=978-0199671595}}</ref>  In 1999, one of the Oxford projects placed the first British-built hardware on the surface of Mars, albeit unwittingly.<ref name=Marsbook>{{cite book |last1=Taylor |first1=Fredric W. |title=The scientific exploration of Mars |date=2010 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |isbn=978-0521829564}}</ref>

Taylor was the author of twelve books on atmospheric and planetary physics.<ref>See his comment underneath http://www.theambler.co.uk/2012/03/05/mapping-the-world-and-beyond/</ref> In September 2011, he retired from full-time academia and from the Halley Professorship of Physics.<ref name="bio - Oxford Physics">{{cite web|title=Fred Taylor|url=http://www2.physics.ox.ac.uk/contacts/people/taylorf|website=Department of Physics|publisher=University of Oxford|accessdate=16 March 2016}}</ref> He died on 16 December 2021.<ref name=":0" />
